stimulus.text:
United States aircraft production, 1940-1944 (number of aircraft built each year).

| 1940 | 6,086 |
| 1941 | 19,433 |
| 1942 | 47,836 |
| 1943 | 85,898 |
| 1944 | 96,318 |
stimulus.source_note: Figures from The Army Air Forces in World War II, vol. VI, chapter 10 (official U.S. government history). Total wartime production was nearly 300,000 military aircraft.

source: original; stimulus table from The Army Air Forces in World War II, vol. VI, ch. 10
stem: The table best supports which of the following conclusions about the American economy during the war?

options.text: Aircraft production grew by the same amount every year
options.misconception: The yearly jumps differ: about 13,000, then 28,000, then 38,000, then 10,000.

options.text: The United States built most of its aircraft before Pearl Harbor
options.misconception: Only about 25,000 of the 1940-1944 total were built before December 1941.

options.text: Aircraft production peaked in 1942 and then declined
options.misconception: Production kept rising after 1942 and peaked in 1944.

options.text: American industry expanded output many times over within four years

rationales.A: The table shows uneven jumps, not equal ones: the rise from 1943 to 1944 is far smaller than the rise from 1941 to 1942.
rationales.B: Production in 1940 and 1941 together was about 25,000 planes, a small share of the five-year total.
rationales.C: The numbers rise every year in the table, from 47,836 in 1942 to 96,318 in 1944.
rationales.D: Output rose from about 6,000 planes in 1940 to about 96,000 in 1944, roughly sixteen times as many.
rationales.general:
1. Read the first and last rows: about 6,000 planes in 1940 and about 96,000 in 1944.
2. Divide the two: 1944 output was roughly sixteen times the 1940 output.
3. The middle years climb every year, so the rise was steady growth, not one lucky year.
4. A sixteenfold rise in four years means industry expanded on a scale peacetime never saw.
Remember: to judge growth, compare the first and last values, then check the years between them.
